lead: Gram–Schmidt turns any basis into an orthonormal basis. Fix e₁ along u₁. For each later vector, subtract its parts along the unit directions already fixed, then scale what remains to length one. The result is a set of perpendicular unit vectors that spans the same space. Orthonormal coordinates make projections, least-squares equations and QR factorization simple. Engineers use the process in computer graphics, signal processing and statistics, and it is the first algorithm in most numerical linear algebra courses.
prereq: You need: inner products and norms from Chapter 5.1, orthonormal sets from Chapter 5.3, and basis and span from Unit 2.

blocks.text: Start with a basis u₁, …, uₙ of a real inner-product space. Write ⟨x, y⟩ for the inner product and ‖x‖ = √⟨x, x⟩ for the length. The output is an orthonormal basis e₁, …, eₙ: each ‖eᵢ‖ = 1 and ⟨eᵢ, eⱼ⟩ = 0 for i ≠ j.
v₁ = u₁, e₁ = v₁/‖v₁‖; for k = 2, …, n: vₖ = uₖ − Σ (i = 1 to k−1) ⟨uₖ, eᵢ⟩ eᵢ, then eₖ = vₖ/‖vₖ‖
blocks.where: uₖ is the k-th input basis vector; eᵢ is the i-th unit direction already fixed; ⟨uₖ, eᵢ⟩ is a scalar coefficient; vₖ is the part of uₖ left after the earlier directions are removed; ‖vₖ‖ is its length.

items: Set v₁ = u₁ and normalize: e₁ = v₁/‖v₁‖.
For k = 2, subtract the shadow along e₁: v₂ = u₂ − ⟨u₂, e₁⟩e₁, then e₂ = v₂/‖v₂‖.
For k = 3, subtract the shadows along e₁ and e₂: v₃ = u₃ − ⟨u₃, e₁⟩e₁ − ⟨u₃, e₂⟩e₂, then e₃ = v₃/‖v₃‖.
Continue to k = n. At each step use all earlier unit vectors e₁, …, eₖ₋₁.

blocks.text: The subtraction is a projection. The vector ⟨uₖ, eᵢ⟩eᵢ is the shadow of uₖ along the unit direction eᵢ. Removing every shadow leaves a vector perpendicular to all earlier eᵢ.

Check orthogonality. For j < k, ⟨vₖ, eⱼ⟩ = ⟨uₖ, eⱼ⟩ − Σ (i = 1 to k−1) ⟨uₖ, eᵢ⟩⟨eᵢ, eⱼ⟩. Only the i = j term survives, and ⟨eⱼ, eⱼ⟩ = 1. So ⟨vₖ, eⱼ⟩ = ⟨uₖ, eⱼ⟩ − ⟨uₖ, eⱼ⟩ = 0. Thus vₖ is perpendicular to e₁, …, eₖ₋₁. Dividing by the positive number ‖vₖ‖ keeps it perpendicular to them and makes its length 1, so eₖ is orthogonal to e₁, …, eₖ₋₁ with ‖eₖ‖ = 1.

Check span. At step k, every eᵢ is a combination of u₁, …, uₖ. Conversely uₖ = vₖ + Σ (i = 1 to k−1) ⟨uₖ, eᵢ⟩eᵢ, and vₖ = ‖vₖ‖eₖ, so uₖ is a combination of e₁, …, eₖ. Hence span{e₁, …, eₖ} = span{u₁, …, uₖ}. The dimension rises by one at each step, so vₖ ≠ 0. If vₖ were zero, uₖ would lie in the previous span, contradicting independence.
At k = n the two spans are the whole space. The set e₁, …, eₙ is therefore an orthonormal basis.

sections.h3: Unnormalized form and a computer note

blocks.text: You can avoid early normalization. Set vₖ = uₖ − Σ (i = 1 to k−1) (⟨uₖ, vᵢ⟩ / ⟨vᵢ, vᵢ⟩) vᵢ, then eₖ = vₖ/‖vₖ‖. The coefficient is ⟨uₖ, vᵢ⟩/‖vᵢ‖²: it uses the earlier orthogonal vector vᵢ, not the original uᵢ. With unit vectors the coefficient is simply ⟨uₖ, eᵢ⟩. Both forms give the same eₖ in exact arithmetic.

In floating point, modified Gram–Schmidt subtracts one direction at a time: first remove the e₁ part from uₖ, then the e₂ part from the updated vector, and so on. It costs about the same and loses less accuracy on a computer.

figure.caption: The first vector is normalized; each later vector loses its parts along the unit directions already fixed before it is normalized. Notice that the subtraction uses e₁ and e₂, not the original u's.

spec.title: Gram–Schmidt on three vectors
spec.aria: A vertical flow that normalizes the first vector, subtracts its part from the second, normalizes again, subtracts both parts from the third, and normalizes once more.

examples.question: Apply the Gram–Schmidt process to u₁ = (1, 1, 0), u₂ = (1, 0, 1), u₃ = (0, 1, 1) in ℝ³ with the standard dot product. Produce the orthonormal basis e₁, e₂, e₃.

traps: Subtracting ⟨u₃, u₁⟩u₁ instead of ⟨u₃, e₁⟩e₁. The coefficient must go with the unit vector that is already fixed.
Writing the coefficient as ⟨uₖ, vᵢ⟩/‖vᵢ‖ instead of ⟨uₖ, vᵢ⟩/‖vᵢ‖². The denominator is the squared length of the orthogonal vector vᵢ; with unit vectors the coefficient is simply ⟨uₖ, eᵢ⟩.
Using u₂ after it has been changed. Keep the original input vectors; only eᵢ are normalized.
Forgetting that order matters: a different order of the same u's gives a different orthonormal basis.
Stopping when vₖ = 0. For an independent set this cannot happen; if it does, the input set was dependent.

quiz.q: Write the Gram–Schmidt formula for vₖ and eₖ.
quiz.a: vₖ = uₖ − Σ (i = 1 to k−1) ⟨uₖ, eᵢ⟩eᵢ; eₖ = vₖ/‖vₖ‖, with v₁ = u₁ and e₁ = v₁/‖v₁‖.

quiz.q: Why must vₖ be nonzero when u₁, …, uₙ are independent?
quiz.a: If vₖ = 0, then uₖ is a linear combination of e₁, …, eₖ₋₁, hence of u₁, …, uₖ₋₁. That contradicts independence.

quiz.q: Apply one step to u₁ = (1, 0, 0), u₂ = (1, 1, 0).
What happens if you run the process on u₁ = (1, 0), u₂ = (2, 0)?
quiz.a: e₁ = (1, 0); v₂ = (2, 0) − 2(1, 0) = (0, 0). The process stops: the input set is dependent.

quiz.q: Given e₁ = (1/√2, 1/√2, 0) and u₂ = (0, 1, 1), find v₂ before normalization.
State the span property at step k.
Why is modified Gram–Schmidt preferred in code?
quiz.a: It subtracts one direction at a time from the current vector, so rounding errors are not amplified as much. Classical Gram–Schmidt can lose orthogonality on nearly dependent vectors.

beyond: Not for the exam. In production numerical software, QR factorization is usually computed by Householder reflections, not raw Gram–Schmidt, because reflections are more stable. Modified Gram–Schmidt still appears in Krylov methods and in algorithms for large sparse systems. Search for 'modified Gram-Schmidt', 'Householder QR', and 'loss of orthogonality' if you want the numerical-analysis view.
